name: CJC-1295

lead: CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone. Users take it to raise growth hormone and IGF-1 for recovery, fat loss, skin and sleep, and some younger users hope it adds height.

It binds the GHRH receptor on the pituitary, increasing growth hormone secretion, and the long-acting version attaches to albumin so one dose lifts GH and IGF-1 for days. Early human studies in healthy adults showed prolonged GH and IGF-1 rises. No published trial has shown muscle, fat-loss or cosmetic changes in healthy people.

paras: Used as an injectable research peptide, often combined with the ghrelin mimic ipamorelin, and reported by forum users as prescribed by some clinics. Users usually describe sleep and recovery changes first, with body-composition goals over months.

Not an approved medicine, sold as a research peptide, and banned in sport. A phase II trial was halted after a participant died, though the physician thought it was likely unrelated to the drug. Reported effects include flushing, headache, water retention and injection-site reactions. Long-term safety is unknown and the status of compounded versions has been in flux.

angle.text: CJC-1295 is an injectable peptide taken to raise growth hormone and IGF-1, aiming at better recovery and sleep and a leaner, younger-looking physique. Human data come from a few endocrine studies showing raised GH and IGF-1. The appearance claims rest on user reports.

lead: CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH, also called growth hormone-releasing factor) developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies. In its best-known form, CJC-1295 with a 'drug affinity complex' (DAC), the peptide attaches to the blood protein albumin, which extends its half-life to roughly six to eight days and allows a single injection to raise growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) for days.[1][2][3] A shorter-acting version without the DAC, often called 'modified GRF (1-29)', is a separate compound, though the two are sometimes confused.[1]

Human trials in healthy adults showed prolonged GH and IGF-1 stimulation, but development for lipodystrophy in people with HIV and for growth hormone deficiency ended after a phase II trial was halted following the death of a participant.[1][4] The attending physician thought the death was most likely due to previously undiagnosed coronary artery disease and unrelated to the drug, but the research was stopped as a precaution.[1] No published trial has shown muscle, fat-loss or cosmetic benefit from CJC-1295 in healthy people.

CJC-1295 is not an approved medicine. It is sold as a research peptide and reported by forum users as prescribed by some clinics, often combined with the ghrelin-mimetic ipamorelin, and it is prohibited in sport.[5][6][7] Recent reviews of peptide use in sport and aesthetics describe human evidence as scarce and note risks associated with mislabeled or contaminated products.[8][7]
infobox: GH raised 2- to 10-fold for 6 days or more; IGF-1 raised for 9 to 11 days after a single dose[1]

paras: CJC-1295 is a modified form of the first 29 amino acids of GHRH (the sequence also known as sermorelin) with four amino acid substitutions that make it resistant to enzymatic breakdown, and the DAC version carries a maleimidopropionyl-lysine group at the C-terminus that bonds to albumin after injection.[1][9][10] Wikipedia notes that the terms CJC-1295, CJC-1295 DAC and CJC-1295 with DAC are synonymous, whereas 'modified GRF (1-29)' (CJC-1295 without DAC) lacks that group and has been wrongly equated with it in some scientific papers.[1] Mass-spectrometry work has identified CJC-1295 in unknown pharmaceutical preparations seized by Norwegian authorities, and doping-control laboratories have developed detection methods for it.[11][12]

CJC-1295 binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells and increases GH secretion, and in rats the albumin-bound analogue was shown to be long-lasting.[10] In humans, one analysis describes a half-life of about eight days for the albumin-binding form.[3] Unlike a continuous GH infusion, studies found that pulsatile GH secretion persisted during continuous stimulation by CJC-1295, with baseline levels raised.[3] After a single dose, plasma GH may increase two- to tenfold for six days or longer and IGF-1 may increase by 0.5- to 3-fold for nine to eleven days; with repeated dosing IGF-1 stayed elevated for up to 28 days.[1][2] Studies also found changes in serum protein profiles consistent with activation of the GH/IGF-1 axis.[13]

Two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind ascending-dose trials of 28 and 49 days in healthy adults aged 21 to 61 (published 2006) examined the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and safety of CJC-1295 and reported prolonged stimulation of GH and IGF-1 secretion.[2] A companion study reported that pulsatile GH secretion persisted during continuous stimulation, and another described once-daily administration in healthy adults.[3][14] A later analysis of the same research program described serum protein profile changes in normal adults.[13]

A phase II trial (NCT00267527) of CJC-1295 in HIV patients with visceral obesity began in 2005 and was terminated; Wikipedia attributes the termination to the death of a participant that the investigator considered probably unrelated to treatment.[4][1]

No trial has assessed CJC-1295 for muscle growth, athletic performance, body composition or cosmetic outcomes in healthy adults. A 2026 narrative review of peptide therapy for orthopaedic and sports medicine states that human evidence for the CJC-1295 plus ipamorelin combination is limited, and a review of aesthetic and endocrine peptides concludes that further studies are needed before most newer peptides can be used safely in humans.[5][15]

Sources reviewed describe the long-term safety of CJC-1295 as unknown. Reviews of peptide use in sport warn of cardiovascular strain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and psychiatric instability associated with growth hormone-axis agents used outside trial conditions, and note that products from an unregulated supply chain are often mislabeled or contaminated.[7] A review of approved and unapproved peptides in sports medicine said rigorous human safety data for unapproved peptides are scarce and potential for serious harm exists.[8]

One forum user describes pronounced hunger and a 'hypo' feeling when combining CJC-1295 with GHRP-6.[16] A netnographic study documented female users' concerns about estimating dose, cycling and long-term consequences given sex differences in GH pulses.[17]

subs.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: A 2016 netnographic study of internet forums found female users well versed in polypharmacy with performance and image drugs who chose CJC-1295 for weight loss, muscle enhancement, youthful skin, improved sleep and injury healing.[17] On T Nation, posters describe running CJC-1295 with ipamorelin or GHRP-6; one user reports using it after a distal biceps tendon surgery, another describes a clinic prescribing the CJC-1295 and ipamorelin pair, and another credits a CJC/ipamorelin/GHRP-2 blend plus kisspeptin for a return of libido.[18][6][16][19]

GHRH analogues are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and analytical papers describe immunoaffinity and mass-spectrometry methods developed to detect CJC-1295 and related peptides in blood and urine.[12][7]
